ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) --  Violence echoed across a volatile Pakistani province and an adjacent tribal region on Saturday, with dozens reported killed in the latest military push, a drone strike, and a car bombing targeting a school bus. A Pakistani girl displaced by the military's offensive against the Taliban rests at a camp Saturday north of the capital. Pakistan's artillery and airstrikes against Taliban militants in North West Frontier Province left 47 suspected militants dead in operations over the last 24 hours, the military said. "Security forces are closing in from different directions and have been able to inflict more casualties," the military said in the daily roundup of its offensive in the Swat district and adjoining regions. The troops have been fighting to oust militants from districts across Pakistan's North West Frontier Province. Forty-five people were killed in various areas of Dir, where four militants were arrested. The military conducted search-and-destroy operations in Shangla district, where they targeted terrorist hideouts and reported the arrest of one militant leader and the death of another. In Swat, the military said it killed a militant commander and were getting closer to the city of Mingora, where they isolated and blocked "the movement of fleeing terrorists," amid the sound of intense exchanges of fire.  Watch Pakistani troops pound Taliban positions » . In the adjacent tribal region, a missile believed fired by a drone overnight struck a madrassa, a religious school, a Pakistani intelligence official said. More than 20 people were killed, according to local and Taliban sources. The strike was near the village of Mir Ali in North Waziristan, one of seven districts in Pakistan's tribal regions. The official asked not to be identified because he is not authorized to speak to the media. According to a count by CNN, this is the 16th suspected missile strike in Pakistan this year. Pakistan has complained repeatedly about what it says are American airstrikes on its territory. The U.S. military in Afghanistan has not commented on the strikes, which typically target Taliban fighters in the border region. But the United States is the only country operating in the region known to have the capability to launch missiles from remote-controlled drones. In Peshawar, at least nine people were killed and 33 hurt Saturday when a car bomb exploded while a school bus passed on a road, local authorities said. The school bus was carrying handicapped children. It is not clear if any of them were killed, but as many as seven were injured. Peshawar is the capital of North West Frontier Province. More than a million people have been displaced in northwestern Pakistan as a result of the two-week-old military offensive with the Taliban, the U.N. refugee agency said Saturday. Antonio Guterres, high commissioner for refugees, said 1,171,682 people have been registered as internally displaced people. These are in addition to the 553,916 displaced people who've fled eruptions of fighting in the tribal areas and North West Frontier Province since August. CNN's Reza Sayah contributed to this report.

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) — Deadly violence spread through an unstable province in Pakistan and a neighboring tribal area on Saturday, as officials reported scores of deaths from a new phase of military operations, a suspected drone attack, and a car bomb that exploded near a school bus.

At a camp north of Pakistan’s capital on Saturday, a girl uprooted by the army’s campaign against the Taliban was seen resting.

Pakistan’s military said artillery fire and air attacks against Taliban fighters in North West Frontier Province had killed 47 suspected militants during the previous 24 hours. In its daily update on the offensive in Swat district and nearby areas, the military said security forces were advancing from multiple directions and had succeeded in causing additional militant casualties.

Pakistani troops have been battling to drive militants out of districts throughout North West Frontier Province. In Dir, 45 people were reported killed in several locations, and four militants were taken into custody. In Shangla district, the army carried out search-and-destroy missions aimed at militant hideouts, reporting that one militant leader had been captured and another killed.

In Swat, military officials said troops killed a militant commander and were moving nearer to the city of Mingora. They said forces had cut off and contained “the movement of fleeing terrorists” as heavy gunfire exchanges continued. CNN also referenced video of Pakistani forces striking Taliban positions.

In the neighboring tribal belt, a missile thought to have been launched overnight by an unmanned drone hit a madrassa, or Islamic religious school, according to a Pakistani intelligence official. Local and Taliban sources said more than 20 people died in the attack. The strike occurred near Mir Ali, a village in North Waziristan, one of the seven districts that make up Pakistan’s tribal areas. The intelligence official requested anonymity because he was not permitted to speak with reporters.

By CNN’s tally, the attack was the 16th suspected missile strike inside Pakistan that year. Pakistan has repeatedly objected to what it describes as U.S. airstrikes on Pakistani soil. The U.S. military in Afghanistan has generally declined to comment on such strikes, which usually target Taliban militants along the border. However, the United States is the only country known to be operating in the area with the ability to fire missiles from remotely piloted drones.

Elsewhere on Saturday, in Peshawar, local officials said at least nine people were killed and 33 wounded when a car bomb detonated as a school bus traveled along a road. The bus was carrying children with disabilities. Authorities said it was unclear whether any of the children died, though as many as seven were injured. Peshawar is the capital of North West Frontier Province.

The U.N. refugee agency said Saturday that more than 1 million people had been forced from their homes in northwestern Pakistan because of the military offensive against the Taliban, which had been under way for two weeks. U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Antonio Guterres said 1,171,682 people had been registered as internally displaced. That figure was in addition to 553,916 people displaced since August by outbreaks of fighting in the tribal areas and North West Frontier Province.

CNN’s Reza Sayah contributed to the report.

# Pakistan presses Taliban offensive as civilian toll mounts

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan —** Pakistani forces intensified their offensive against Taliban militants in the country’s northwest, killing 47 suspected militants in the latest operations, military officials said, as the humanitarian crisis deepened with more than 1.1 million people displaced by the fighting.

The military campaign, focused on Taliban strongholds in and around the Swat Valley and neighboring districts, has become one of Pakistan’s most significant efforts in years to push back militants who had expanded their control across parts of the North West Frontier Province.

Pakistani security officials said airstrikes and ground operations targeted militant positions, hideouts and supply routes. The military reported that 47 suspected militants were killed in clashes and bombing raids, though the figures could not be independently verified because access to the conflict zone remained heavily restricted.

The offensive comes as Pakistan faces growing international pressure to confront Taliban fighters who have used territory in the northwest as a base for attacks inside Pakistan and across the border in Afghanistan. The United States has repeatedly urged Islamabad to take stronger action against extremist networks operating in the tribal areas and beyond.

## Drone strike kills more than 20 at madrassa

In a separate incident, more than 20 people were killed in a suspected U.S. drone strike on a madrassa, or Islamic religious school, in Pakistan’s tribal region, local officials and intelligence sources said.

The strike reportedly targeted a compound believed to have been used by militants. Pakistani intelligence officials said several suspected Taliban-linked fighters were among the dead, though local residents said civilians may also have been killed.

The United States rarely comments publicly on drone operations in Pakistan, but missile strikes by unmanned aircraft have become an increasingly frequent and controversial tool against militant leaders in the country’s remote border areas.

Pakistani leaders have publicly criticized the drone attacks, saying they violate national sovereignty and fuel anti-American sentiment. Privately, U.S. and Pakistani cooperation on counterterrorism has often been reported, though both governments have been reluctant to discuss details.

## Violence hits Peshawar

Militant violence also continued in Peshawar, the provincial capital and a key gateway to Pakistan’s northwest. Authorities said nine people were killed in an attack in the city, underscoring the Taliban’s ability to strike beyond the front lines of the military offensive.

Peshawar has been hit repeatedly by bombings, shootings and attacks on security forces, government offices and supply convoys. The city has also become a major destination for families fleeing the fighting in Swat, Buner and Lower Dir.

Security was tightened across the city following the latest deaths, with police checkpoints increased on main roads and near government buildings.

## More than 1.1 million displaced

The United Nations and Pakistani officials said the number of internally displaced people had risen to more than 1.1 million, making it one of the largest internal displacements in Pakistan’s recent history.

Families have fled by truck, bus, car and on foot, many carrying only clothing, bedding and basic belongings. Camps have been established in several districts, but aid officials said many displaced people are staying with relatives or in schools, mosques and temporary shelters.

Relief agencies warned that the scale of the crisis was straining resources. Clean water, sanitation, medical care and food supplies remained urgent needs, particularly for children and the elderly.

“This is a rapidly growing humanitarian emergency,” one aid official said. “The fighting is moving faster than the response capacity on the ground.”

The Pakistani government has appealed for international assistance, saying it needs help providing shelter, health care and food to displaced families.

## Offensive seen as a test for Pakistan

The campaign against the Taliban is widely viewed as a major test of Pakistan’s civilian government and military leadership. Earlier peace deals with militants in Swat collapsed after Taliban fighters advanced into nearby districts, raising alarm in Islamabad and abroad.

Under the now-defunct agreement, authorities had allowed the implementation of Islamic law in parts of Malakand Division in exchange for an end to Taliban violence. Instead, militants expanded their influence, prompting criticism that the government had ceded territory to extremists.

The military now says it is determined to clear militants from the region. Officials have urged civilians to leave areas where fighting is expected, but the mass exodus has created severe hardship and raised concerns about how long public support for the operation can be sustained.

Analysts say the government must not only defeat militants militarily but also restore basic services, courts, police and civilian administration in areas once held by the Taliban.

“If people return to the same conditions that allowed the Taliban to rise in the first place, the operation will not be enough,” said a Pakistani security analyst.

## Civilian concerns grow

Human rights groups have urged both the military and militants to protect civilians. The Taliban has been accused of using populated areas for cover, while airstrikes and artillery by government forces have raised fears of civilian casualties.

The government says it is taking precautions, but officials acknowledge that fighting in mountainous and densely populated areas presents serious risks.

For displaced families, the immediate concern is survival. Many said they fled after hearing explosions, seeing militants in their villages or being warned that military action was imminent.

“We left everything behind,” one displaced resident from Swat said. “We do not know when we can go home, or whether our home will still be there.”

As the offensive continued, Pakistani officials insisted the operation would go on until Taliban fighters were driven from the area. But with casualties rising, cities under threat and more than a million people uprooted, the conflict has already become one of the most consequential chapters in Pakistan’s battle against militancy.

**Escalating violence grips northwest Pakistan, officials say, as civilians flee fighting near tribal belt**

**By [Reporter Name], CNN**  
**PESHAWAR, Pakistan — [Date]**

Violence across Pakistan’s northwest intensified this week as security forces battled militants in areas bordering Afghanistan, leaving civilians dead, forcing families from their homes and prompting fresh warnings from humanitarian agencies about worsening conditions for displaced residents.

Pakistani military officials said troops launched operations in parts of the former tribal areas and the North West Frontier Province — now known as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa — after a series of militant attacks on security posts, police stations and government installations. The clashes are among the latest signs of deteriorating security in a region long affected by insurgent networks, cross-border militancy and military counterterrorism campaigns.

In a statement, the Pakistani military said security forces had “engaged terrorist elements” in several districts and had killed multiple suspected militants. The statement said troops recovered weapons, ammunition and communications equipment during raids, but did not provide independent confirmation of casualties.

“Security forces remain committed to eliminating the threat of terrorism and restoring peace to the affected areas,” the military said.

Local officials, however, said the fighting has taken a heavy toll on civilians. A senior district administration official in the northwest, speaking on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to brief the media, said artillery fire, roadside bombs and militant attacks had disrupted daily life in several towns and villages.

“People are frightened. Markets have closed in some areas, schools are not operating normally, and many families have moved to safer locations,” the official said.

### Civilian casualties reported

Local hospital officials said they had received wounded civilians from areas affected by the violence. Doctors at a government hospital in the region said several women and children were among those treated for shrapnel and gunshot injuries.

One local health official said ambulances had struggled to reach remote villages because of blocked roads and security restrictions.

“Some of the injured arrived hours after the incident because families could not safely travel during the fighting,” the official said.

Civilian casualty figures remain difficult to verify independently due to limited media access, intermittent communications and restrictions imposed during military operations. Local officials said at least several civilians had been killed in recent days, though the number could rise as reports emerge from remote areas.

Residents described nights filled with explosions and gunfire.

“We left with only the clothes we were wearing,” said one displaced resident who arrived with his family on the outskirts of Peshawar. “The children were crying all night. We did not know where the shells were landing.”

### Displacement grows

Refugee and humanitarian agencies say the renewed violence has triggered another wave of displacement from villages near the tribal belt. A refugee agency official said thousands of people had moved toward safer districts, joining relatives or seeking temporary shelter in schools, mosques and makeshift camps.

The UN refugee agency and local relief organizations have previously warned that families displaced by conflict in Pakistan’s northwest often face shortages of food, clean water, medical care and shelter. Aid workers say women, children and elderly residents are especially vulnerable.

A humanitarian official familiar with relief operations said registration teams were trying to assess new arrivals but faced access challenges.

“Movement is fluid. Some families leave for a few days and return, while others cannot go back because their homes are damaged or the fighting continues,” the official said. “The needs are growing faster than available resources.”

### Militants target security forces

Pakistani security officials said militants have increasingly targeted police and paramilitary forces in the region, using ambushes, improvised explosive devices and suicide attacks. The mountainous terrain and porous border with Afghanistan have historically made the area difficult to secure.

Authorities have blamed militant factions operating from remote hideouts, including groups aligned with the Pakistani Taliban. Militant groups have not always claimed responsibility for individual attacks, and CNN cannot independently verify the identities of those involved in the latest clashes.

Pakistan has repeatedly accused militants of using Afghan territory as a staging ground for attacks, an allegation Afghan authorities have denied or downplayed in the past. The issue has added strain to relations between Islamabad and Kabul.

### Government vows response

Provincial officials said police reinforcements had been deployed to vulnerable areas and security checkpoints were being expanded. The provincial government said it was coordinating with federal authorities to support displaced families and ensure medical supplies reach affected districts.

“The protection of civilians is our top priority,” a provincial government spokesperson said. “Relief teams have been instructed to provide immediate assistance where access is possible.”

Rights groups have urged both militants and security forces to protect civilians and allow humanitarian access. They have also called for transparent investigations into civilian deaths and damage to homes and public infrastructure.

For many families in Pakistan’s northwest, the latest escalation has revived memories of previous waves of conflict that displaced millions over the past two decades.

“We have lived through this before,” said a tribal elder from an affected area. “Every time there is fighting, ordinary people suffer first. We want security, but we also want to live in our homes without fear.”
